judgment_terms: reasonable measures to protect against unauthorized access or use
proposed.condition: The landlord, manager, Handoff or a collector keeps, for a business purpose, consumer information about a tenant (a consumer report, such as the move-in screening report, or any record derived from one) and discards it, or sells, donates or transfers the equipment or media that store it (for example when a tenancy file is closed).
proposed.effect: It disposes of the information by reasonable measures to protect against unauthorized access or use: policies it follows and monitors for burning, pulverizing or shredding papers, or destroying or erasing electronic media, so the information cannot practicably be read or reconstructed; or a contract, after due diligence, with a record-destruction business it monitors. A service provider holding the information for the landlord follows the same measures. Aggregate data that identifies no one is outside the rule. The rule creates no duty to keep or destroy records that other law does not impose. State disposal law does not govern this conduct (US:15USC1681t(b)(1)(F)-furnisher-preemption); the rest of the file follows NY:GBL-399-h-disposal.
proposed.quote: (a) Standard. Any person who maintains or otherwise possesses consumer information for a business purpose must properly dispose of such information by taking reasonable measures to protect against unauthorized access to or use of the information in connection with its disposal.

construction.quote: (b) “Consumer information” means any record about an individual, whether in paper, electronic, or other form, that is a consumer report or is derived from a consumer report.

proposed.reasoning: 15 U.S.C. 1681w directs the FTC's rule for non-bank persons; 682.2(b) reaches any person under FTC jurisdiction that possesses consumer information for a business purpose, which includes landlords, managers and collectors.

judgment_terms: related transactions (a series the recipient knows or has reason to know is connected)
proposed.instrument: Internal Revenue Code, information returns (26 U.S.C. ch. 61 subch. A pt. III)
proposed.actor: landlord; manager; Handoff (whoever receives the cash in its business)
proposed.condition: In the course of its business the landlord, its manager or Handoff receives more than $10,000 in cash from a former tenant or someone paying for it (for example a move-out balance or arrears paid in currency), in one transaction or in related transactions (any within 24 hours, or a series the recipient knows or has reason to know is connected).
proposed.effect: The recipient files Form 8300 stating the payer's name, address and TIN, the amount, and the date and nature of the transaction, by the 15th day after the cash is received (for installments, once the payments received within 12 months exceed $10,000), and furnishes the payer a written statement by January 31 of the next year. Cash means currency, including foreign currency and digital assets; a personal check drawn on the payer's own bank account is not cash; a cashier's check, bank draft, traveler's check or money order of $10,000 or less counts only in a designated reporting transaction (a retail sale of consumer durables, collectibles or travel, which rent is not) or where the recipient knows it is being used to avoid reporting. No one may structure payments to avoid the return.
proposed.quote: (2) who, in the course of such trade or business, receives more than $10,000 in cash in 1 transaction (or 2 or more related transactions), shall make the return described in subsection (b) with respect to such transaction (or related transactions) at such time as the Secretary may by regulations prescribe.

construction.quote: The reports required by this section must be filed in accordance with the Form 8300 instructions and related publications by the 15th day after the date the cash is received.
The term related transactions means any transaction conducted between a payer (or its agent) and a recipient of cash in a 24-hour period.

proposed.reasoning: Section 6050I(a) and (e) set the duty and the payer statement; 26 CFR 1.6050I-1 sets the 15-day filing time, the related-transaction and installment rules, and the definition of cash, whose monetary-instrument branch reaches only designated reporting transactions (retail sales of consumer durables, collectibles and travel or entertainment).

proposed.instrument: Internal Revenue Code, information returns (26 U.S.C. ch. 61 subch. A pt. III)
proposed.actor: payment settlement entity; Handoff or a manager by configuration
proposed.condition: A former tenant pays rent or a balance by payment card or through a third party payment network (a payment app or platform), and the payment is settled for the owner. Configuration (a): the settlement goes directly to the owner's merchant or network account (or the manager's account for that one owner). Configuration (b): Handoff (or a manager) receives settlements for several owners through one account and distributes them to the owners. Configuration (c): Handoff contracts with the settlement entity to make the settlement payments on its behalf (electronic payment facilitator).
proposed.effect: (a) The merchant acquiring bank (cards) or the third party settlement organization (networks) files Form 1099-K for the owner; the landlord files no information return on those payments, and they are not reported as rent on Form 1099-MISC (US:26CFR1.6041-1-agent-reports-rent). (b) Handoff (or the manager) is an aggregated payee: it is the participating payee toward the settlement entity and the payment settlement entity toward each owner it pays, so it files Form 1099-K for each owner for the calendar year and furnishes each owner a statement by January 31; for card payments with no minimum, for network payments only where an owner's payments exceed $20,000 and 200 transactions. (c) Handoff files the return in place of the settlement entity. Which configuration applies is an operating choice.
proposed.quote: (ii) such intermediary shall be treated as the payment settlement entity with respect to the settlement of such transactions with the participating payees.

construction.quote: (1) the amount which would otherwise be reported under subsection (a)(2) with respect to such transactions exceeds $20,000, and (2) the aggregate number of such transactions exceeds 200.

proposed.instrument: Internal Revenue Code, information returns (26 U.S.C. ch. 61 subch. A pt. III)
proposed.actor: landlord (payor in its trade or business)
proposed.condition: In its trade or business the landlord pays $600 or more in a calendar year to an attorney in connection with legal services, for example a settlement or judgment on a former tenant's deposit claim paid to the tenant's attorney or by a check payable jointly to the tenant and the attorney.
proposed.effect: The landlord files an information return (Form 1099-MISC, gross proceeds paid to an attorney) for the attorney for the whole amount paid and furnishes the attorney a statement, unless the payment is the attorney's own fee for services to the landlord (reported under 6041) or another listed exception applies. The part of the payment that is income to the tenant is reported for the tenant under 6041 when it reaches the 6041 threshold (US:26CFR1.6041-1-agent-reports-rent sets it: $2,000 for payments after 2025): returning the tenant's own deposit is not income (US:26CFR1.166-1(e)-bad-debt), while damages above it, including the punitive part of a twice-the-deposit award, are gross income of the tenant.
proposed.quote: (A) In general This subsection shall apply to any payment to an attorney in connection with legal services (whether or not such services are performed for the payor).

construction.quote: makes payments aggregating $600 or more during a calendar year to an attorney in connection with legal services (whether or not the services are performed for the payor) must file an information return for such payments.
The mere fact that the payments were extracted from the wrongdoers as punishment for unlawful conduct cannot detract from their character as taxable income to the recipients.

proposed.reasoning: Section 6045(f) and 26 CFR 1.6045-5 require the attorney return at $600; the regulation's examples require a separate 6041 return for the claimant where the payment is the claimant's income. Punitive and statutory damages are gross income (Commissioner v Glenshaw Glass, 1955; 26 U.S.C. 61(a)); the return of the tenant's own trust money is not.
